title: Nigeria exceeds OPEC quota for 5th month as oil production hits 1.71m barrels in September
text:
Nigeria’s total daily average production of crude oil and condensate rose to 1,717,030 barrels per day (bpd) in September 2026,
Nigeria’s total daily average production of crude oil and condensate rose to 1,717,030 barrels per day (bpd) in September 2026, marking a 2.34 per cent increase from August levels, as the country consolidated its standing as Africa’s top oil producer.
Data released by the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) shows that single-day production hit a high of 1.84 million barrels during the month, while the lowest daily volume recorded was 1.68 million barrels.
Excluding condensates, Nigeria’s strict crude oil production averaged 1.53 million barrels per day (mbpd) in September. This performance represents 102 per cent of its 1.5 mbpd target set by the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
With this output, Nigeria has now met or exceeded its assigned OPEC quota for five consecutive months. Data from the regulator shows crude production reached 1.53 mbpd in May; 1.55 mbpd in June; 1.51 mbpd in July; 1.50 mbpd in August; and 1.53 mbpd in September.
According to industry figures, the sustained production momentum was primarily anchored on operational stability across major producing assets, supported by the absence of critical pipeline outages during the review period.
Enhanced uptime and crude evacuation efficiency across key export channels enabled upstream operators to maintain reliable production flows.
“The improved performance was primarily driven by stable production operations across most producing assets and the absence of any major pipeline outages during the period under review. This enhanced operational stability supported improved production uptime and crude evacuation efficiency.
“The sustained growth recorded in September reflects the continued commitment of operators and industry stakeholders towards improving operational efficiency, maintaining asset integrity, and enhancing production reliability across the Nigerian upstream petroleum sector,” the commission stated.
A detailed analysis of daily average crude and condensate output across key export terminals shows that the Forcados Terminal led production volumes, accounting for 320,320 barrels per day (kbpd) during the review month.
The Bonny Terminal followed closely as the second-largest stream, delivering a daily average of 303,270 barrels.
Heineken Lokpobiri, Nigeria’s Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (oil), who had earlier commented on the increased production, attributed the growth to ongoing policy reforms and renewed investor confidence in the nation’s energy sector.
He recalled that when the Tinubu- led administration came on board in 2023, the country barely produced a million barrels, inclusive of condensates. Lokpobiri attributed the poor production to operational bottlenecks in the upstream sector, which he said were driven by the Commission.
“For anything to be done in the upstream, NUPRC has to approve it. And there were delays, bottlenecks, and so what we did was to engage NUPRC.
“And I told the then leadership that you’re not going to be judged by the number of bottlenecks you impose but by the number of barrels that you enable. You’re also going to be judged only by the number of businesses you enable, not by the number of regulations that you introduce, which also constitutes another disincentive to investment.
“And collaboratively, we came together, found solutions and things changed for the better. Today we’re doing, as of yesterday when you sent the report to me, we’re doing 1.821 million barrels a day. That is over 80 percent of success,” he said in an earlier engagement.
Lokpobiri also attributed the production increase to the ‘unprecedented’ level of drilling campaign going on in the industry, which he said has led to over 70 active rigs. He added that the drilling campaign is critical if Nigeria must achieve its 3 million barrels target.
“Our ambition to do 3 million barrels will be a mirage unless we have a sustainable and increasing campaign in this industry.
“NUPRC has done well in five years. Please continue on this trajectory of rendering excellent services that will guarantee sustainable growth in this industry. Do the best you are doing to ensure that we are not sent back to Egypt,” he added.
Lokpobiri further emphasised that Nigeria’s geographical advantage in the Gulf of Guinea has insulated it from geopolitical disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, making it a prime destination for diverted global capital.
He emphasised that to capitalise on this opportunity and attract dollar investments, Nigeria must guarantee a predictable operating environment, a globally competitive regulatory framework, and superior fiscal terms relative to other investment climates.
BusinessDay, established in 2001, is a daily business newspaper based in Lagos — the only Nigerian newspaper with a bureau in Accra, Ghana. It publishes both daily and Sunday titles, circulating across Nigeria and Ghana.

title: NVIDIA Run:ai Is Now Open Source as Part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform | NVIDIA Technical Blog
text:
Accelerate innovation across the DSX ecosystem and bring AI factory solutions to market faster with the open foundation for AI workload and GPU orchestration.
By Ekin Karabulut and Sam Heywood
NVIDIA is releasing the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform as open source software, expanding the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform with a foundation for AI workload and GPU orchestration.
The release includes four modular components that can be adopted independently: KAI Scheduler for GPU-aware Kubernetes scheduling, GPU Fractioning Operator for CUDA-native GPU sharing, KAI Resource Management for organizational quota and hierarchy, and Workload Map for a consistent workload-management contract.
Eight NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners including Crusoe, Mirantis, Nebius, OpenNebula Systems, Rafay, Saturn Cloud, Spectro Cloud, and vCluster are integrating the open source platform into their offerings.
NVIDIA is making the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform available as open source software, giving customers, developers, and ecosystem partners access to production-grade AI workload and GPU orchestration capabilities. This release expands the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform by establishing NVIDIA Run:ai as an open foundation that enables the broader ecosystem to bring differentiated solutions to market faster in response to evolving customer needs.
Over the past several years, NVIDIA Run:ai has helped organizations run AI workloads on Kubernetes at scale by dynamically allocating GPU resources and managing workloads across the full lifecycle, from data processing and training to inference.
By open sourcing NVIDIA Run:ai platform capabilities as part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory, it is now possible for every NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner and AI cloud to increase workload throughput, improve GPU utilization, and operate shared AI infrastructure more efficiently and effectively.
This post details the open source release, which includes the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform and four components that can also be adopted independently: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator , KAI Resource Management , Workload Map . Together with additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. Platform teams and ecosystem partners can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole, build on it for their own products and services, or integrate individual components based on their requirements.
NVIDIA Run:ai can be adopted directly as open source software or through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner offerings.
Deploy the open source platform directly
The complete source code for NVIDIA Run:ai is available in the NVIDIA Run:ai repository within the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization . Teams can inspect the code, contribute to its development, build on top of the platform or adopt its modular components independently.
The complete open source NVIDIA Run:ai platform is also available on NVIDIA NGC as a Community Product, with a Helm chart for installing the integrated stack.
Note: The NVIDIA Run:ai source code is governed by its applicable open source licenses. Downloading the Community Product from NGC requires acceptance of the applicable NVIDIA Software License Agreement and Product-Specific Terms for NVIDIA AI Products. No paid NVIDIA Run:ai subscription or NVIDIA support entitlement is required for the Community Product, and NVIDIA enterprise support is not included.
Adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners
Open source NVIDIA Run:ai gives NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners direct access to AI workload and GPU orchestration innovations they can use in their own NVIDIA DSX AI factory solutions. By adopting the complete platform or integrating individual components, partners can bring those innovations to market faster and respond more quickly to evolving customer and operational requirements.
Crusoe integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with Crusoe Managed Kubernetes, combining GPU workload orchestration with managed Kubernetes and GPU infrastructure.
Mirantis extends k0rdent AI with NVIDIA Run:ai to deliver a lifecycle-managed, Metal-to-Model AI factory stack that automates infrastructure provisioning and maximizes GPU utilization.
Nebius offers NVIDIA Run:ai as a one-click application deployment in Nebius AI Cloud, giving customers a streamlined way to deploy and operate the complete platform on Nebius Managed Service for Kubernetes.
OpenNebula Systems integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with the OpenNebula AI Cloud Platform through OneKS, combining GPU workload orchestration with infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle management for open and sovereign AI clouds.
Rafay is expanding its NVIDIA Run:ai integration to deliver it as a fully managed service. Rafay automates the entire stack, from GPU infrastructure and clusters to the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane and tenants, so AI cloud providers and enterprises can offer it through their own self-service catalogs.
Saturn Cloud integrates NVIDIA Run:ai to help AI cloud operators launch white-label AI inference services through its Token Factory platform, combining GPU orchestration with dedicated and multi-tenant model serving, per-token metering, and automated billing.
Spectro Cloud integrates NVIDIA Run:ai into PaletteAI, enabling customers to deploy it through PaletteAI Studio and manage it with the same lifecycle automation used across their AI infrastructure.
vCluster provides NVIDIA Run:ai through pre-validated deployment templates that stand up a complete environment per tenant, allowing operators to strengthen tenant boundaries while NVIDIA Run:ai continues to schedule across one GPU fleet.
For NVIDIA Enterprise AI Factory deployments, NVIDIA Run:ai continues to be available through NVIDIA-supported commercial offerings including as a standalone product, through NVIDIA Mission Control and NVIDIA AI Enterprise, and select cloud marketplaces. Availability, licensing, and support terms vary by offering.
For teams that already have a platform and need to fill a specific capability gap, the following sections describe when and how to use each modular component independently.
Modular open source components of the NVIDIA Run:ai platform
This section details the four components included in the open source release: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, and Workload Map. With additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. You can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole or integrate individual components based on your unique requirements.
KAI Scheduler: The scheduling engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai
KAI Scheduler is the Kubernetes-native scheduler that powers the NVIDIA Run:ai platform. NVIDIA released KAI Scheduler as open source software under the Apache 2.0 license and contributed it to CNCF as a Sandbox project. KAI remains the upstream engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai, and all scheduler development happens in the community repository, so every improvement flows through the same codebase. NVIDIA continues to support the project’s maintainers and work with the broader ecosystem to advance AI workload scheduling at scale.
KAI Scheduler is purpose-built for GPU workloads at scale, coordinating:
Gang scheduling with prescheduling in-memory simulation, so multipod jobs are placed all-or-nothing and aren’t evicted needlessly
Fair-share (including time-based fair-share) and quota allocation that keeps resource shares balanced across teams
Topology awareness and bin-packing at the scheduling-decision level
GPU sharing, which allows multiple workloads to share single or multiple GPUs (MIG, MPS, time sharing, HAMi, CUDA 13.4 MPS fractioning)
Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) support
To learn more about key features, visit the kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler GitHub repo.
Use KAI Scheduler for diverse AI workloads that require fair access to cluster resources and topology-aware placement. It can be deployed in an existing cluster alongside the current software stack without requiring the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform.
Follow the project, ask questions in the #kai-scheduler channel on CNCF Slack, and contribute on the kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler GitHub repo.
GPU Fractioning: An operator for GPU fractions on Kubernetes
The NVIDIA Run:ai platform has long supported fractional GPU allocation, enabling multiple workloads to share a GPU with hard memory isolation. Fractions can be requested on demand and set up on the fly, with no per-node setup from an administrator in advance. It is one of the most widely used capabilities among ML teams running workloads that do not require the full memory of a GPU, including interactive notebooks and inference for smaller models. NVIDIA Run:ai pioneered that experience with a proprietary implementation.
GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and the proprietary implementation has been retired in favor of the native capability available in CUDA 13.4 . The CUDA driver enforces a hard limit on GPU memory for each workload, and each workload sees only the GPU memory allocated to its fraction. What is still needed is a clean way to consume it on Kubernetes. This is what GPU Fractioning Operator provides: an operator that enables CUDA GPU fractions on a cluster, along with a metrics exporter for per-pod visibility into fractions in use. It is a Kubernetes integration layer that allows workloads to use CUDA-native fractioning, and it is scheduler-agnostic.
Use the GPU Fractioning Operator for workloads that can share underutilized GPU capacity, including notebooks, development sessions, and smaller models. GPU Fractioning Operator integrates with KAI Scheduler to translate available GPU capacity into an actual placement decision, while remaining compatible with other schedulers.
GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA 13.4-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and integrates with KAI Scheduler. To get started, refer to the GPU Fractioning Operator documentation .
KAI Resource Management: The organizational layer
While the scheduler decides how work is placed, KAI Resource Management governs who gets what:
Projects and departments: The organizational structure, or “org layer,” that maps resources to the teams and initiatives that consume them.
Resource management with an organizational hierarchy: The ability to allocate, guarantee, and share GPU capacity across that org structure, with fair-share and quota semantics.
Node pools: Grouping and targeting of heterogeneous hardware so workloads land on the right resources.
Together, these let platform teams move beyond raw Kubernetes scheduling and manage GPUs the way organizations actually operate: by team, by department, by initiative, and by resource guarantee.
Use KAI Resource Management for heterogeneous clusters shared by multiple teams that require defined shares of capacity. For example, a platform team could guarantee 50% of the cluster to research while preventing any one team from monopolizing the remaining capacity. If you are already tracking quota entitlements in a spreadsheet or hand-maintaining namespaces per team, this is the layer that replaces it. It can be combined with KAI Scheduler in your clusters.
Read more about how these concepts map to real deployments in the KAI Resource Management documentation .
Workload Map: A workload-management contract for Kubernetes
Workload Map is the contract NVIDIA Run:ai uses to support any workload type. KAI Scheduler uses it for scheduling and gang semantics; the rest of the platform uses it for workload discovery, monitoring and lifecycle management.
In Kubernetes, an AI workload is almost never a bare Deployment or Job. It is a PyTorchJob, a RayCluster, a JobSet, a KServe InferenceService, a Dynamo graph deployment, or a company’s own custom resource. Each type has its own internal structure, components with different roles (driver and workers, head and workers, prefill and decode), its own scaling and gang semantics, and its own way of reporting status.
Workload Map provides a consistent way to treat these workloads as first-class objects throughout their lifecycle:
Scheduling with gang and topology awareness
Observing status and health consistently
This workload-management layer sits between Kubernetes primitives and the schedulers, dashboards, SRE and troubleshooting tools, cost tools, backup tools, and ML platforms that serve users. Instead of each tool building a private, partial integration for every CRD, Workload Map defines each workload type once so any platform or tool can schedule, observe, act on, and govern it consistently without hardcoding each CRD.
Use Workload Map for platforms and tools that must understand and manage multiple Kubernetes workload types without hardcoding each CRD. It ships as a Go library that works offline on unstructured objects, so you can adopt it without adding anything to your cluster. It is deliberately narrow: Workload Map describes workload structure and does not schedule, queue, autoscale, or propagate across clusters.
Learn more in the dsx-ai-factory/workload-map GitHub repo and check out the adopter projects .
The following open source projects address complementary AI infrastructure challenges. They can be adopted independently or incorporated into broader solutions that include the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform or selected components.
Model Streamer: Reducing cold-start latency
Cold-starting an inference workload on Kubernetes can take several minutes, during which time GPUs are allocated but idle for a single step: loading model weights from storage onto the GPU. Model Streamer reads weights concurrently and streams them directly into GPU memory, cutting load time for large models.
Since its release, Model Streamer has been adopted across the inference stack, including by inference engines, cloud providers and storage platform vendors.
Model Streamer is integrated upstream in vLLM and SGLang , where it can be enabled with the --load-format runai_streamer flag, as well as in ModelExpress . Support covers local filesystems, S3-compatible stores, and network file shares alongside several cloud backends detailed below.
Major cloud providers now document Model Streamer in their own guidance.
AWS : Model Streamer ships in the vLLM Deep Learning Container and is the recommended fast path in the official EKS documentation for running AI/ML inference , with tuned concurrency and chunk sizing for S3 .
Google Cloud : Native Cloud Storage support built in collaboration with NVIDIA , including GKE documentation for streaming straight from a bucket into accelerator memory.
Microsoft Azure : Azure Blob Storage integration, jointly developed by Microsoft and NVIDIA Run:ai to provide first-class model streaming for Azure customers. Published benchmarks on eight NVIDIA H100 VMs shows 3x-6x faster loading than the default loader and a steady 80 Gbps, compared with approximately 40 Gbps for the default path.
Several AI data infrastructure partners have independently benchmarked Model Streamer and published their results:
WEKA loaded into GPU memory in just 3.5 seconds, roughly 40% faster than loading from local NVMe—enabling organizations to build petabyte-scale shared model repositories that accelerate model readiness without the time, effort, and capacity required to maintain duplicate model copies across the inference environment.
VAST Data measured 1.7 seconds, a 60% improvement over loading from local NVMe
DDN streamed the 65.5 GB Qwen3-32B across 8 GPUs in under four seconds, and translated it into cost: saving up to 10% of daily GPU runtime compared to using local storage.
Use Model Streamer when starting new replicas and loading model weights is the primary bottleneck.
Grove: One API, any inference architecture
Emerging workload patterns—including agentic pipelines, disaggregated serving and mixture-of-experts training—consist of multiple connected components that must scale together. Grove provides a Kubernetes API for orchestrating these workloads, from a single pod to deployments spanning tens of thousands of GPUs.
Grove provides topology-aware autoscaling and hierarchical gang scheduling, allowing components such as prefill and decode to start as all-or-nothing units. On NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 , it also manages ComputeDomain resources automatically, enabling multinode NVLink performance through a single annotation instead of hand-authored YAML.
Grove is a modular part of NVIDIA Dynamo that can be used independently, and it already powers training and inference pipelines at scale across a range of companies. Recent work includes support for llm-d and Volcano as a scheduler backend, with Kueue support in progress.
Use Grove for graph-based workloads with distinct roles and coupled scaling requirements.
Get started with open source NVIDIA Run:ai
NVIDIA Run:ai is available now as open source software in the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization. To learn more and get started, check out these resources:
We’re excited to bring this work to the community and to build the next generation of AI workload and GPU orchestration in the open. We welcome your contributions, issues, and feedback.
Ekin Karabulut is a data scientist and developer advocate previously at Run:ai, now at NVIDIA, exploring the efficient usage of large models in different production scenarios. Previously she worked on privacy implications of federated learning, focused on distributed training techniques and got fascinated by inefficiencies in GPU usage in research and industry settings. She established the AI Infrastructure Club and is based in Munich, Germany.
Sam Heywood is director of Product Marketing at NVIDIA, focused on AI infrastructure, GPU orchestration, and Kubernetes technologies that help organizations build and operate AI at scale. His technology interests include accelerated computing, cloud-native infrastructure, distributed AI workloads, and the systems that enable efficient training and inference. Sam brings extensive experience in enterprise technology and product marketing, translating complex technical capabilities into clear strategies for customers and the market. He holds a bachelor’s degree in Computer Science from The University of Texas at Austin and an MBA.

title: Nvidia opens up Israeli-founded Run:ai software two years after $800 million acquisition
text:
Nvidia opens up Israeli-founded Run:ai software two years after $800 million acquisition
The chip giant is making the AI workload management platform open source, giving developers and cloud providers access to tools designed to improve the use of costly GPUs.
Nvidia is making the full software platform of Israeli-founded Run:ai available as open source, giving developers, cloud providers and other technology companies access to tools designed to make more efficient use of the expensive graphics processing units powering the artificial intelligence boom.
The move opens up technology Nvidia acquired in late 2024 for an estimated $800 million, following an eight-month regulatory review in the United States and Europe. Run:ai develops software that helps organizations allocate computing resources across AI workloads, from training models to running them in production. As demand for AI computing has surged, the ability to extract more work from existing hardware has become an increasingly important part of the industry’s infrastructure.
The newly open-sourced platform allows organizations to examine and adapt the code, use the complete system or adopt individual components. Nvidia is also making the software available through its developer infrastructure, while a number of cloud and infrastructure providers are integrating it into their own offerings.
The announcement follows a commitment made when Nvidia acquired Run:ai. At the time, the companies’ founders, Omri Geller and Dr. Ronen Dar, said they planned to open-source the software to help developers build AI systems faster. They argued that making the platform available as open source could extend its reach beyond Nvidia’s own GPUs and into the wider AI ecosystem.
Founded in 2018, Run:ai developed a software layer that manages how AI workloads use GPUs, the processors that have become central to training and operating modern AI models. Rather than allowing different teams and applications to compete for computing resources without coordination, the platform can allocate capacity dynamically, including sharing GPU resources among workloads that do not require an entire chip.
The open-source release includes the complete Run:ai platform as well as four components that can be adopted separately: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management and Workload Map. Together, they cover different parts of the process, from deciding which workloads run on which resources to dividing GPU capacity and allocating it among teams.
The release does not mean that every use of Run:ai is now free of charge or includes enterprise support. The community product does not require a paid Run subscription or Nvidia support entitlement, but enterprise support is not included, and the software remains subject to its applicable open-source licenses and other terms. Nvidia will continue to offer commercial versions through its enterprise AI products and supported cloud offerings.

title: Apple, Nvidia lead list of tech companies that donated to Trump’s White House ballroom project
text:
Some of the biggest tech companies donated tens of millions of dollars for the construction of the White House ballroom.
By Matt Binder
Matt Binder joined Mashable's tech vertical in 2018, where he covers social media, tech policy, cybersecurity, online scams, cryptocurrency, AI, creator news, weird tech, and other related tech beats.
Here are the tech companies that gave millions to Donald Trump's White House ballroom – and just how much they donated..
Some of the world's biggest tech companies donated tens of millions of dollars for the construction of President Donald Trump's White House ballroom — and now we know exactly how much money they gave to the White House, too.
According to a new report from the Washington Post , Apple and Nvidia topped the list of donors to Trump's ballroom project, giving $25 million each for the president's pet project. The two tech companies were among the top four donors overall, alongside the Adelson Family Foundation and Charles Ergen, the co-founder of Dish Network.
However, Apple and Nvidia were far from the only tech companies to make massive donations for the ballroom.
Google provided $22 million, via a settlement the company made with Trump related to the shutdown of his YouTube channel following the events of Jan. 6, as Mashable reported previously.
Microsoft donated $10 million, and Palantir was right behind them with a near $10 million donation of their own.
Amazon, Meta, and T-Mobile donated $5 million each.
A number of cryptocurrency companies like Coinbase, Ripple, and the Winklevoss twins, who represent their Gemini crypto exchange, also donated $5 million. Crypto exchange Kraken donated $1 million.
HP and Micron each gave the president $2.5 million and Salesforce donated $2 million.
Non-tech companies like defense contractors and the former CEO of Marvel's foundation also gave tens of millions of dollars to the ballroom project.

title: 'This computer is going to be incredible': Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang explains why the new Surface Laptop Ultra is "really a work of love"
text:
'This computer is going to be incredible': Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang explains why the new Surface Laptop Ultra is "really a work of love"
By Mike Moore
Nvidia CEO sings the praises of the new Surface Laptop Ultra
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has sung the praises of Microsoft's new Surface Laptop Ultra , describing it as "so beautiful" and "incredible".
Speaking at a developer event in London, Huang outlined the development process that went into building the hardware powering the new product, which is the first Microsoft device powered by an Nvidia chip.
“This computer is going to be incredible - it took us four years to build it," Huang told attendees including TechRadar Pro , "this project is really a work of love - we had several thousand engineering years dedicated to it, we build a brand new revolutionary chip, a whole new line of PCs, it’s so beautiful - you’re going to love it.”
The end of the traditional PC?
Revealed in September 2026, the Surface Laptop Ultra is targeted towards developer and AI usage, powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform with an N1X processor and RTX Blackwell graphics, supporting up to 128GB unified memory
This is alongside 24GB RAM and 512GB storage, while the next version has 32GB RAM and 1TB storage, making it ideal for creators, AI specialists, engineers, scientists, developers, and other users running demanding applications.
But as Huang tells it, the creation of the device, set to launch on October 16 2026, was a long and arduous process.
“It took four years to do this," Huang said of the hardware development process. "We were thinking about agentic systems, AI and autonomous systems, and how they’ll be able to access your files, and be grounded on information, and be able to reason about it and use tools - but the ultimate tool is your personal computer, right?"
"So wouldn’t it be cool if we could create a personal computer, a PC that actually runs an agent locally - so it can go off and just work on things for you - and not only could it just run locally, it would be smart enough to use the tools."
Huang explained his vision of "texting" your PC to ask for help, to get it to do tasks like rendering images and updating slides, then delivering them straight to you.
"Wouldn’t it be awesome if you could just text your computer - you don’t have to bring it with you anymore - just leave it at your desk!”
“So we created this thing - it took us four years to do it, so I called Satya (Nadella, Microsoft CEO), and the two of us talked about it…and so we had to create a brand new chip, we had to wait until Blackwell was done - and this thing has 1 petaflops of computing, and because we knew the models were going to be big, we had to redesign how the GPU uses memory - so this is the first Nvidia GPU with shared memory, one petaflops, Blackwell architecture - and also it has to run everything a PC doesn’t.”
“There’s three types of PCs, right," Huang outlined, "there’s the PC that basically you use to type in - that’s called a PC, there’s the Nvidia gaming PC, you’ve got GeForce in that, and you’ve got the Nvidia workstations that runs all kinds of applications…so we figured that if you’re going to have an AI go use the tools, it should be able to use every single tool…it runs everything, it runs every AI framework, it runs any AI model as well."
Mike Moore is Deputy Editor at TechRadar Pro. He has worked as a B2B and B2C tech journalist for over a decade, including at one of the UK's leading national newspapers and fellow Future title ITProPortal. When he's not keeping track of all the latest enterprise and workplace trends, he can most likely be found watching, following or taking part in some kind of sport.

title: RTX 5090 Shipments Worth $500,000 Vanished Into Thin Air At São Paulo Airport, Distributor Says This Has Never Happened In Nearly Four Decades Of Operation
text:
Two pallets of ZOTAC-made RTX 5090 GPUs arrived at the Guarulhos International Airport terminal in São Paulo, worth around $500,000, but according to the latest report, the flagship GPU shipments had gone missing after a distributor filed a complaint. After seeing the ravenous demand for NVIDIA’s flagship GPU, its launch price of $1,999 climbed to a whopping $5,000–$7,000, making it an opportunity of a lifetime for criminals who want to sell the top-end graphics card at a premium through online marketplaces.
The estimated $500,000 figure only covers the cost of the actual RTX 5090 shipment; retail pricing could be significantly higher.
At a cost of R$ 2.5 million, Oderço, a distributor based in Maringá, in the state of Paraná, will be fuming after it learned about the incident. Shortly after the RTX 5090 shipment was nowhere to be found, the news spread rapidly thanks to a public video posted on Oderço’s social media accounts by its president, Oderço Matos. He has stated that the company is still seeking clarification and has not received any information that would help locate the merchandise.
The distributor says it has contacted the relevant parties to investigate and is demanding answers about what happened to the goods. According to Times Brasil, Matos mentioned that the company has been importing products since 2008, making it a period of nearly two decades—not once in the company’s 38-year operational history has it ever lost or misplaced a shipment, until now. The remark underscores how unusual the company considers the incident and frames the loss as a departure from an otherwise clean track record.
Sadly, much about the case remains unclear. For instance, the account provided by the distributor does not explain how the pallets disappeared, when in the airport’s handling chain they were lost, or who might be responsible. The report also does not mention any police investigation, statement from the airport operator, or response from customs or logistics providers. Until those parties comment, the only version of events available is the company’s own.
With its 32GB of GDDR7 VRAM and 1.79TB/s of memory bandwidth, the RTX 5090 will be a godsend for anyone wanting to experience AAA 4K gaming or, at the very least, run small- to mid-sized AI models at excellent prompt-processing and token-generation speeds. In short, it’s easy to conclude why a shipment of NVIDIA’s latest and greatest GPU would be in the crosshairs of those trying to score big, even if it’s at the expense of distributors like Oderço.
Only recently, there were reports that the RTX 5090 was being discontinued as the GPU disappeared from NVIDIA’s marketplace . Thankfully, the company responded, stating that the claims are untrue , but as you can tell, its sheer demand will attract the wrong kind of attention. For now, the latest episode raises questions about security and traceability in the handling of high-value electronics at one of Latin America’s busiest airports. Whether the missing pallets are recovered and whether authorities or the airport’s operators explain what went wrong will determine how the story develops.

title: Nokia advances AI-RAN toward commercial deployment and physical AI, launches sovereign agentic AI platform for telco autonomy with NVIDIA
text:
Nokia advances AI-RAN toward commercial deployment and physical AI, launches sovereign agentic AI platform for telco autonomy with NVIDIA
New capabilities improve radio performance, enable real-time intelligence at the edge and extend governed AI agents across network operations.
Nokia AI-native anyRAN software and NVIDIA accelerated computing turn the radio access network into a distributed platform for sensing, intelligence and real-time action.
BT, Deutsche Telekom, Elisa and Orange provide growing evidence of AI-RAN progress among European operators.
dApps and an expanding infrastructure ecosystem extend the platform for physical-AI and edge-AI applications.
Nokia today announced the next step in how it is bringing AI-native networks to commercial reality with NVIDIA, with new capabilities that apply AI within radio processing, support intelligence close to where data is generated and extend governed AI agents for cross-domain network operations. Building on the industry’s first commercial AI-RAN platform, announced in July, AI-RAN is being integrated into live networks and moving closer to deployment. Together, Nokia and NVIDIA are creating the real-time network foundation needed for physical-AI applications while giving operators a practical path to improve today’s 5G and 5G Advanced networks and evolve to AI-native 6G.
Customer progress moves AI-RAN closer to deployment
One year ago, Nokia and NVIDIA formed a partnership to add NVIDIA-powered, commercial-grade AI-RAN products to Nokia’s radio access network portfolio. The companies are now applying AI within the 5G signal-processing chain, including channel estimation, beamforming, multi-user MIMO pairing and scheduling. Nokia AI-native anyRAN software, running on NVIDIA Aerial RAN Computer, provides a software-defined foundation for integrating AI-powered radio functions that improve network capacity and performance.
The next era of connectivity will be defined by networks that do far more than connect: They will distribute intelligence, continuously optimize performance and enable entirely new AI-powered services, including the emerging world of physical AI. Together with NVIDIA and leading operators, Nokia is turning this vision into reality by bringing AI into the radio network and across network operations. This creates a trusted, software-defined foundation that helps operators get more from their spectrum today while enabling new Physical AI use cases and opening a practical path toward increasingly autonomous, AI-native 6G networks.
The next generation of telecommunications infrastructure will be built on a software-defined architecture. NVIDIA and Nokia are combining CUDA accelerated computing and AI with Nokia’s network software and expertise to improve radio performance and deploy trusted AI agents. Together, we are advancing software-defined, AI-native 5G and laying the foundation for 6G.
Recent customer activity provides growing evidence of deployment progress:
In Helsinki, Elisa ran voice, mobile data and video analytics simultaneously on the same AI-RAN platform in its 5G network, demonstrating how AI-RAN can support radio and AI workloads in a live network environment. Distributed deployment and the evaluation of customer use cases and commercial AI-RAN services are expected in 2027.
BT is preparing to deploy a live-network trial in Birmingham in 2027.
Deutsche Telekom and Nokia are developing AI-based channel estimation as part of a broader set of AI-driven capabilities to improve network performance and efficiency. While this is just one element of the broader AI-RAN opportunity, initial laboratory measurements showed typical uplink throughput improvements of 10–15%, with greater gains under more complex radio conditions. The next phase will extend this work with additional AI spectral-efficiency algorithms and field validation.
Orange plans to progress on testing AI-RAN in both lab and real network conditions.
Together, these customer programs are part of a broader platform built around three capabilities: AI-led spectral efficiency to extract more capacity from existing spectrum; integrated sensing and communications to help the network understand the physical environment; and localized inference to process intelligence close to where data is generated.
An open ecosystem for AI-RAN applications and deployment
In addition to its work with telecommunications providers, Nokia is extending its AI-RAN ecosystem through distributed applications (dApps) that run at the network edge and enable new services. Nokia’s E3 interface gives these applications real-time access to RAN data, turning the radio network into a programmable platform for sensing and localized intelligence. Using dApps:
DeepSig, a pioneer in AI-native wireless communications, is developing spectrum-sensing software that uses existing radio infrastructure to identify RF threats, interference and rogue transmitters.
ZaiNar, a Physical AI company building real-time spatial intelligence technology, is integrating its positioning software with Nokia Cloud AI-RAN to enable precise, network-based location capabilities using existing wireless infrastructure, without requiring changes to connected devices or radio hardware.
At NVIDIA GTC Berlin, Nokia is demonstrating integrated sensing and communications, showing how the RAN can detect and understand activity in the physical environment. Nokia and NVIDIA are working with a growing infrastructure ecosystem to provide the deployment foundation for these capabilities:
Dell Technologies, Quanta Cloud Technology and Supermicro are supporting flexible NVIDIA Aerial RAN Computer configurations for distributed and centralized deployments that run Nokia 5G anyRAN software alongside AI inference workloads.
Red Hat is bringing AI-RAN technologies onto a common cloud-native platform with Red Hat OpenShift, creating a secure foundation for RAN functions and AI workloads on shared infrastructure.
Sovereign agentic AI platform for telco autonomy, co-created by Nokia and NVIDIA
Nokia and NVIDIA are also advancing their collaboration on agentic AI for trusted, sovereign, cross-domain network autonomy. NVIDIA AI Enterprise software and NVIDIA Nemotron models and libraries are being integrated into Nokia’s agentic platform, allowing operators to build, evaluate, deploy and operate telco-specific agents across radio, core, transport and cloud networks. Nokia provides the network intelligence, operational context and governance needed for agents to understand network conditions and take controlled action. Glass-box autonomy maintains operator oversight, while agentic guardrails govern how actions are tested and executed.
The combined architecture, integrated with NVIDIA open models and libraries, supports on-premises, cloud and hybrid deployments, giving operators control over where operational data, models and policies reside. It extends the Nokia and NVIDIA collaboration from AI in the radio network to autonomous operations, creating a common foundation to optimize the RAN, support AI workloads close to where data is generated and enable low-latency autonomy across network domains. Several telecommunication providers, including etisalat UAE, MEO and Airtel, are working with Nokia to identify advanced use cases and integration timelines.
High-performance solutions that link distributed AI infrastructure
At GTC, Nokia will also showcase high-performance IP and optical solutions required to link distributed AI infrastructure. Nokia’s data center connectivity, IP gateway and wide-area networking solutions, including 800G coherent pluggables, help cloud and AI builders scale connectivity across a diverse and growing set of data center locations. By connecting radio, edge and data-center resources as one coordinated infrastructure environment, Nokia’s technology supports AI workloads everywhere.

title: How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage | NVIDIA Technical Blog
text:
By Andrew Hoyle
NVIDIA KvikIO provides high-level Python and C++ interfaces that sit above the cuFile C API to enable accelerated file I/O into GPU memory.
The library and cuFile make independent path-selection decisions: KvikIO chooses whether to invoke cuFile, while cuFile determines whether the transfer uses the accelerated nvidia-fs kernel module or a CPU-staged compatibility path.
Runtime settings such as KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE and KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD control KvikIO's behavior, and cufile.json settings such as execution.parallel_io and execution.min_io_threshold_size_kb shape how cuFile decomposes and schedules requests.
Per-process cuFile statistics collected with CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 and inspected via gds_stats reveal whether operations traveled the nvidia-fs accelerated path (nvfs counters) or the compatibility path (posix counters).
KvikIO is part of the NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries for data science and has been used to accelerate I/O in cuDF, cuCIM digital pathology workflows, cuPhoton scientific-image analysis, and GPU-accelerated Presto analytics workloads.
GPU applications are processing ever-growing datasets with increasingly powerful accelerators. According to the 2025 Stanford AI Index , compute for notable AI models has been doubling approximately every five months, while the size of datasets used to train LLMs has been doubling approximately every eight months. As computation and data scale together, moving data efficiently from storage becomes a necessity for keeping accelerators supplied.
NVIDIA Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this challenge by enabling a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory. This avoids unnecessary staging through CPU memory and reduces overall CPU utilization in the system. GDS is supported by a growing ecosystem that includes many major storage vendors .
At the application layer, Python plays a central role in modern AI development. As of August 2025, nearly half of all new AI projects on GitHub were built primarily in Python while the main application interface to GDS is the cuFile C API.
NVIDIA KvikIO , a Python and C++ library for high-performance file I/O, bridges this gap. It provides high-level, idiomatic Python and C++ interfaces, along with additional controls over how I/O requests are performed.
The tutorial in this post demonstrates how to use the NVIDIA KvikIO Python API to configure storage I/O, read data into GPU memory, and confirm that the accelerated path within GDS was activated. It also shows how to inspect the KvikIO and cuFile settings that influence the path each operation takes.
How does NVIDIA KvikIO leverage GDS?
GDS is the broader technology that enables accelerated data movement between supported storage and GPU memory. For file system-based storage, cuFile provides the C library and API through which applications and frameworks access GDS. KvikIO sits above cuFile, providing higher-level Python and C++ interfaces along with its own controls over how I/O requests are executed. Figure 1 shows these layers and their two separate path-selection points. Initialization failures, unsupported configurations, and error-handling paths are omitted for clarity.
The application supplies a file system path and GPU buffer, and KvikIO determines whether to send the request through cuFile or use its POSIX compatibility path, which stages the data through host memory. When cuFile is selected, KvikIO registers the file and issues the I/O using the target GPU buffer.
cuFile then determines the actual transfer path based on system support, the file system, and its configuration. It may use the accelerated GDS path or its CPU-staged compatibility path. Therefore, reaching the cuFile API confirms that KvikIO selected cuFile, but does not by itself confirm that the accelerated GDS path was activated.
The following sections walk through how to configure the system, perform a KvikIO read, and verify the resulting path.
Before beginning this tutorial, you will need:
A Linux system with an NVIDIA GPU and GPUDirect Storage installed.
A GDS-supported storage and file system configuration.
Permission to create, read, and write files at the storage endpoint, along with access to GDS tools such as gdscheck and gds_stats .
For complete installation and platform requirements, refer to the NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage documentation .
This tutorial was tested with the following configuration:
An x86_64 system with an NVIDIA H100 GPU, CUDA 13.3, and cuFile 1.18.
A local NVMe device formatted with ext4 .
A PIX connection between the selected GPU and NVMe device, meaning the path traverses at most one PCIe bridge.
IOMMU and ACS disabled to preserve PCIe peer-to-peer transfers.
The nvidia-fs kernel module is loaded to provide the accelerated path.
You can inspect the GPU-to-storage topology with the following command:
Step 1: Set up NVIDIA KvikIO
First, create a Python environment and install the CUDA 13 build of KvikIO. CuPy will be installed as a dependency.
$ python3 -m venv kvikio-env
$ python -m pip install kvikio-cu13
You can verify the installation with the following:
$ python -m pip show kvikio-cu13 cupy-cuda13x
Step 2: Inspect the configuration
Before performing any I/O, inspect the active KvikIO settings and confirm that the system recognizes the GDS components. In the KvikIO defaults API, the compatibility-mode setting is named compat_mode , and its name attribute reports the active mode as AUTO , ON , or OFF . The following commands report the loaded KvikIO and cuFile versions, the active compatibility mode, and the minimum request size KvikIO sends to cuFile:
import kvikio.cufile_driver as cufile_driver
cufile_driver.libcufile_version()
defaults.get("gds_threshold")
On the tutorial system, KvikIO reports compatibility mode as AUTO and a GDS threshold of 16 KiB. AUTO instructs KvikIO to try cuFile and fall back to its POSIX backend if cuFile is unavailable. Reads smaller than the threshold use the KvikIO POSIX path directly. These settings can also be controlled through KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE and KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD . For the complete list, refer to the KvikIO runtime settings .
Next, inspect the GDS platform and cuFile configuration:
$ /usr/local/cuda-13.3/gds/tools/gdscheck.py -p 2>&1 | less -R
The output lists the installed GDS components, supported file systems, detected GPUs, and active cuFile configuration. Figure 2 shows how to inspect the KvikIO and GDS configuration used in this tutorial.
KvikIO settings can also be changed in Python. For example, defaults.set accepts a dictionary to change several settings at once, or a name and value to change one setting:
defaults.set({"task_size": 1024**3, "num_threads": 8})
defaults.set("compat_mode", kvikio.CompatMode.OFF)
Step 3: Read a file into GPU memory
Next, create the input file once before running the Python example. The following command writes a 1 GiB file with random data using direct I/O and flushes it to storage:
of=/mnt/nvme1/kvikio-tutorial/kvikio-example.bin \
bs=1M count=1024 \
The following program allocates a 1 GiB CuPy array in GPU memory and supplies it to KvikIO as the destination buffer:
"/mnt/nvme1/kvikio-tutorial/kvikio-example.bin"
# Allocate a GPU buffer large enough to hold the file.
dtype=cp.uint8,
# Read the file into the GPU buffer.
with kvikio.CuFile(file_path, "r") as file:
bytes_read = file.read(gpu_buffer)
# Validate that 1 GiB was read.
The context manager opens the file and completes the read into GPU memory. Although the return value confirms that the complete file was read, it does not identify the underlying data path.
Step 4: Determine the data path
One way to validate the data path used by any cuFile-based application is to observe the cuFile runtime per-process statistics. These statistics can be enabled by setting CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 and then inspected with gds_stats while the process remains active.
For this KvikIO example, the environment variable keeps the setting scoped to a single run, although it can also be configured in cufile.json .
$ CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 python3 -i read_with_kvikio.py
Running Python interactively keeps the process alive after the read, allowing gds_stats to inspect its accumulated counters.
Figure 3 demonstrates this workflow. In the per-GPU output, nvfs counts operations representing the path taken through the nvidia-fs kernel module, while posix counts operations handled by the cuFile compatibility path.
The KvikIO default 4 MiB task size divides the 1 GiB request into 256 read operations. The per-GPU statistics report n=256 , nvfs=256 , and posix=0 , showing that all 256 operations used the nvidia-fs path.
Step 5: Compare the available paths
The same read can be repeated with different settings to demonstrate the two control layers. First, require KvikIO to use cuFile:
$ CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 \
python3 -i read_with_kvikio.py
On the tutorial system, gds_stats reports nvfs operations, confirming that cuFile selected the accelerated path. Next, force cuFile to use its compatibility path:
KvikIO still calls cuFile, but the operations now appear under posix rather than nvfs . Finally, the KvikIO compatibility mode bypasses cuFile entirely:
python3 read_with_kvikio.py
In this case, KvikIO performs the read through its CPU-staged POSIX backend, so cuFile does not record the operation. The next section examines the cuFile settings that control request execution.
Step 6: cuFile configuration for a KvikIO read
After KvikIO selects its cuFile path, cuFile applies another set of controls that determine how the request is executed. These controls are defined in cufile.json and operate independently of KvikIO runtime settings.
Request decomposition and parallel execution
KvikIO and cuFile can both divide a large operation into smaller pieces. KvikIO applies KVIKIO_TASK_SIZE first, with KVIKIO_NTHREADS controlling how those tasks are scheduled. Each task on the cuFile path becomes a separate cuFile request. Once cuFile receives one of those requests, its execution settings determine whether it can be divided again and processed using the cuFile internal thread pool. The following cuFile settings control this behavior:
Enables cuFile internal parallel processing.
Limits the number of cuFile worker threads available per GPU queue.
Sets a target minimum size for internally scheduled pieces; a final remainder may be smaller.
Limits how much parallelism cuFile prepares for one request.
Limits the number of pending work items in the internal queue.
A 1 GiB read, step by step
The configuration used here has four cuFile worker threads, max_request_parallelism set to four, and min_io_threshold_size_kb set to 8192 (8 MiB). With the KvikIO default 4 MiB task size, a 1 GiB read becomes 256 cuFile requests. Each 4 MiB request is handled as one piece by cuFile. This is the run that produced nvfs=256 in the earlier statistics.
If KVIKIO_TASK_SIZE is set to 1 GiB, KvikIO instead sends one large read request to cuFile. The CuPy destination has not been explicitly registered with cuFile, so cuFile uses its unregistered buffer scheduling path. It limits the request to min (4 worker threads, 4 maximum request parallelism) = 4 pieces.
Dividing 1 GiB four ways gives 256 MiB per piece, already larger than min_io_threshold_size_kb which is 8 MiB. With room in its queue, cuFile assigns three pieces to workers, processes the fourth on the calling thread, and waits for them to finish.
Those 256 MiB pieces are units of scheduled work, not individual storage transfers. Because the destination buffer is not registered for storage DMA, cuFile reads into a registered GPU bounce buffer and copies the data into the destination. Since GDS 1.17, these bounce buffers can be configured as slabs. The nvidia-fs path in this configuration uses slabs no larger than 16 MiB, so each 256 MiB piece is processed through smaller transfers. The 8 MiB scheduling target does not set their transfer size.
When the 8 MiB split target matters
In this configuration, execution.min_io_threshold_size_kb is set to 8192 (8 MiB). That target does not change the 1 GiB split, but it would affect a 16 MiB cuFile request. Four equal pieces would be 4 MiB each, so cuFile schedules two 8 MiB pieces instead. KvikIO must use a task size of at least 16 MiB for cuFile to receive that request intact.
KvikIO in NVIDIA CUDA-X for data science
KvikIO is part of the NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries for data science (formerly RAPIDS). Its development is closely connected to the GDS integration originally built for NVIDIA cuDF GPU DataFrame library, where parallel cuFile reads accelerated Parquet and ORC ingestion. This design was later incorporated into KvikIO, building on the cuDF original GDS data-ingest work .
KvikIO has since been used with GDS in cuCIM digital pathology workflows and in the cuPhoton xDataReader for scientific-image analysis , while related GPU-accelerated Presto work shows benefits of GDS in data analytics workloads. Together, these examples show the broader role of KvikIO as an application-facing I/O layer over the storage acceleration GDS provides.
This tutorial has demonstrated how to read data into GPU memory and use level-three GDS cuFile statistics to distinguish the accelerated nvidia-fs path from CPU-staged compatibility paths. These path decisions matter significantly for popular libraries such as cuDF that use KvikIO for many I/O operations .
The key takeaway is that KvikIO and cuFile make separate decisions. KvikIO selects whether to call cuFile, while cuFile determines the final transfer path and execution strategy. Understanding these layers enables applications to understand the path the I/O is taking and tune the settings that matter for their workload.
Ready to get started? Run the KvikIO Python example featured in this post on your GDS-enabled system. For more examples, explore the C++ and Python KvikIO code in the MagnumIO GDS samples directory . Use gds_stats to check whether reads appear under nvfs or posix , then apply the same verification to your own KvikIO workloads.
Andrew Hoyle is a systems software engineer at NVIDIA, where he measures and improves data movement performance between storage systems and GPUs. On the GPUDirect Storage team, he develops features and works on integrations with software libraries. He holds a master’s degree in Computer Science from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities.

title: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia had record lobbying quarters
text:
OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia had record lobbying quarters
Collectively, they spent nearly $6 million around cybersecurity, child safety, and more.
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.
It was a busy summer for AI lobbyists. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nvidia each had their highest-spending lobbying quarter between July and September, federal disclosures show.
Nvidia spent the most of the group at $2.2 million, followed by Anthropic’s $2.1 million and OpenAI’s $1.5 million. Compared to other Big Tech companies with long-established presences in Washington, the sums aren’t out of the ordinary. Microsoft, for example, has spent at least $2 million a quarter going back to 2021, and Google regularly spends over $3 million, including this quarter. But it’s a clear signal that the three AI firms recognize how important shaping policy has become.
Tech CEOs were already visible fixtures in Washington during this period, with many of them attending a White House lunch with President Donald Trump in late September, which resulted in a “morally binding” AI safety accord that they agreed to. The lobbying disclosures show that even more discussions were happening frequently behind the scenes, during a time just before Trump named his AI czar and task force . With Democrats expected to win back at least some control in Congress after this year’s midterm elections, AI companies may only find it more important to engage with lawmakers who see cracking down on the industry as a winning issue .
Anthropic included a detailed list of bills, executive orders, and other topics it lobbied Congress and the White House about in the third quarter. Among them were AI-related provisions in the Kids Online Safety Act, export control provisions in the AI Overwatch Act, Trump’s executive order renaming AI “Super Intelligence,” and the Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to put energy costs for data centers on their developers.
AI companies are becoming increasingly active in policymaking
OpenAI’s lobbying looks like a response to some of the fallout from the Hugging Face attack , though the disclosures only list high-level topics. In addition to engaging on issues like copyright, OpenAI lobbied Congress, the White House, the Small Business Administration, and the Commerce and State Departments over cybersecurity evaluations for frontier models, AI safety oversight frameworks, and antitrust protections for information sharing. Nvidia lobbied Congress, as well as several different federal agencies and White House offices, on issues including 6G networks, “responsible AI design,” competition policy, quantum computing, and export control policy.
Apple also had a record-breaking quarter, spending $3.1 million and engaging on issues including intellectual property, tariffs, kids online safety, competition, and domestic semiconductor manufacturing. It engaged on bills that seek to put the onus on app stores to verify users’ ages, for example. It’s the first quarter in which Apple has reported spending more than $3 million on lobbying.
The disclosures show that leading AI companies are becoming increasingly active in policymaking, in a quarter that marks a lead-up to the midterm elections. OpenAI didn’t even spend $1 million on lobbying in a single quarter until this year, and it didn’t spend more than half a million until the end of 2024. The most Anthropic spent in a single quarter last year was just over $1 million. And this quarter is the first in which Nvidia has spent more than $2 million. With issues like data center development and AI safety on many voters’ minds, AI lobbyists’ work will likely only increase no matter whichever party has control next year.

title: Which AMD Graphics Card Is Equivalent To The NVIDIA RTX 5070?
text:
Which AMD Graphics Card Is Equivalent To The NVIDIA RTX 5070?
By Diego Perez
The graphics card market has seen extreme shortages over the last year, and many gadgets have been jumping in price because of it. As such, many people are looking at alternatives for the graphics cards they've been eyeing. The RTX 5070 is an incredibly popular GPU, for example, but there are AMD cards that match or even beat its performance at the same price. The closest AMD equivalent to Nvidia's RTX 5070 is the Radeon RX 9070. Both have an MSRP of $549, and they trade blows in benchmarks for AAA games like "Resident Evil Requiem" and "Cyberpunk 2077."
With the GPU market's volatility, however, it's not a fair comparison to make. It's difficult to find GPUs at MSRP these days, and the RTX 5070 can easily reach prices upwards of $1,000. That price point puts it in competition with more powerful AMD cards like the Radeon RX 9070 XT, which outperforms the RTX 5070 considerably in most games.
Radeon RX 9070 vs RTX 5070
The AMD Radeon RX 9070 is the closest equivalent to Nvidia's RTX 5070, and each card achieves similar results in most situations. If you're looking to push high framerates at 1440p or game at 4K with the help of upscaling and frame generation, either GPU will work in your rig. Looking at "Red Dead Redemption 2," the RX 9070 averages 127 FPS at 1440p with Ultra settings (as tested by Linus Tech Tips ). The RTX 5070 gets a respectable 115 FPS average. In "Cyberpunk 2077" on the Ultra preset at native 1440p with ray tracing enabled, the RX 9070 averages 42 FPS while the RTX 5070 has an average of 46 FPS.
There are some situations where AMD beats Nvidia, however. In "Crimson Desert," the RX 9070 pulls in an average of 84 FPS at 1440p without FSR upscaling or frame generation (as tested by Jegs TV ). The RTX 5070 averages just 68 FPS under those same conditions. This also applies to 4K resolution, with AMD's 51 FPS average beating Nvidia's 36 FPS.
The 9070 XT takes things even further
AMD's RX 9070 XT is positioned as a competitor to Nvidia's upgraded RTX 5070 Ti, but the current hardware market changes things. The base RTX 5070 has an MSRP of $549, but you'll have a tough time finding it anywhere at that price. The cheapest available RTX 5070 cards hover around $900, but you can easily find a much faster RX 9070 XT for the same cost.
The 9070 XT is a significant upgrade over the RTX 5070 is every regard. In "Ark: Survival Ascended," at Medium settings, the RX 9070 XT averages 51 FPS with a 1% low of 43 FPS (as reported by Hardware Unboxed ). The RTX 5070 averages only 35 FPS, so even the absolute lowest peak of the 9070 XT's benchmark surpasses the 5070's average frame rate. You'll also see similar patterns in newer games like "Resident Evil Requiem." At 1440p with maxed out settings and ray tracing set to High, the RX 9070 XT averages 153 FPS with a 1% low of 118 FPS. On the RTX 5070, the average is 121 FPS with 1% lows dropping to 96 FPS.
Both GPUs are being sold for roughly the same price at the time of writing. With that in mind, you can essentially get a graphics card as good as the RTX 5070 Ti for the same price as a base RTX 5070 — if you're willing to deal with the disadvantages of buying an AMD GPU instead of Nvidia .
